newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Shots fired in air as Cambodian workers protest.
newsitem.headline: Shots fired in air as Cambodian workers protest.

text.p: Shots were fired in the air when more than 3,000 workers at Cambodia's largest garment factory on Tuesday protested the suspension from work of three employees who formed a union, witnesses said.

Ou Mary, Om Navy and Phuong Sophon, leaders of the Free Trade Union of Khmer Workers, told Reuters they were briefly detained by managers at Cambodia Garments Ltd on Tuesday and told their union, formed on December 10, would not be allowed.
"We work long hours...and we make only $35 per month," said Ou Mary. "We want better conditions."
Their suspension sparked a protest within the factory grounds.
Guards closed the front gates, and when workers tried to pry them open to let in journalists and more workers, guards fired several rounds from automatic weapons into the air.
The protesters dispersed after about two hours.
Analysts said the protest at Cambodia Garments, the top garment producer here, was a sign of growing pains in Cambodia's fastest-growing industry.
"We have to understand it is a growing industry, so when the industry grows, there are always some hiccups along the way," said Van Sou Ieng, who heads the Garment Manufacturers Association.
There are 34 garment factories in Cambodia employing more than 16,000 workers, according to the Industry Ministry.
However, human rights groups have complained that some workers have been treated unfairly.
Last week Thomas Hammarberg, special representative of the U.N. Secretary-General for Human Rights in Cambodia, called working conditions in garment factories appalling.
Hammarberg, who recently visited two garment factories here, said while workers are officially required to put in only eight hours a day, they are pressured to work much more.
He said some laborers fear dismissal if they protest the treatment. He called it "a blackmail situation".
The three union leaders said their suspensions come just one week after they formed a union and three days after they held a small protest.

The protest was led by Sam Rainsy, a former finance minister who was kicked out of the government in 1994 and now heads the opposition Khmer Nation Party, which the government has refused to recognise.
The directors of Cambodian Garments were not available for comment, and workers answering phones at the factory hung up when asked questions.
